## VIII.9 Notes

The Yang-Baxter equation first came up in a paper by Yang [Yan67] as a factorization condition of the scattering S-matrix in the many-body problem in one dimension and in work of Baxter [Bax72] [Bax82] on exactly solvable models in statistical mechanics. It also played an important role in the quantum inverse scattering method created around 1978-79 by Faddeev, Sklyanin, Takhtadjian [Fad84] for the construction of quantum integrable systems. Attempts to find solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation in a systematic way have led to the theory of quantum groups (see [Dri87]). Many papers in the literature are devoted to the construction of R-matrices, e.g., [Dri85] [Dri87] [Jim86a] [Jim86b] [KS80], to quote but a few.

The concept of a quasi-cocommutative and of a braided (or quasi-triangular) Hopf algebra is due to Drinfeld [Dri87] [Dri89a]. For a review, see [Maj90b]. The four-dimensional Hopf algebra of Example 2 of Section 2 is due to Sweedler. The universal $R$ -matrices $R_{\lambda}$ were found by Radford [Rad93a].

The dual concept of cobraided bialgebras appears in [Hay92] [LT91] [Maj91b] [Sch92]. Cobraided bialgebras have properties dual to braided bialgebras. We gave some of them in Exercises 5-7.

The FRT construction is due to Faddeev, Reshetikhin and Takhtadjian [RTF89]. The bialgebras $M_{p,q}(2)$ and $M_{q}(n)$ of IV.10 can be obtained by this method (see Exercise 10). In Sections 5-6 we followed the treatment proposed by [LT91].

Exercise 1 is taken from [Kau91] and Exercise 2 from [Rad93a]. The cobraided Hopf algebra of Exercise 8 was found by Pareigis [Par81] before the advent of quantum groups.

# Chapter IX Drinfeld's Quantum Double

In the previous chapter we showed that braided Hopf algebras provided solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. The problem is now to find enough such Hopf algebras. Drinfeld [Dri87] devised an ingenious method, the "quantum double construction", which builds a braided Hopf algebra out of any finite-dimensional Hopf algebra with invertible antipode. It is the goal of this chapter to describe this construction in full detail, and to show how to apply it to the finite-dimensional quotient of the Hopf algebra $U_{q}(\mathfrak{sl}(2))$ considered in VI.5. We also give a characterization of the modules over the quantum double in Section 5.

## IX.1 Bicrossed Products of Groups

The quantum double construction is a special case of the bicrossed product construction. Since the latter is rather involved, we start with an analogous construction for groups, namely the bicrossed product of groups due to Takeuchi [Tak81]; it generalizes the notion of a semidirect product of groups.

Let G be a group with subgroups H and K. We assume that for any element x in G there exists a unique pair $(y,z)\in H\times K$ satisfying

$$
x = y z.
$$

(1.1)

This allows us to attach to any pair $(y,z) \in H\times K$ a unique element $z\cdot y$

in H and a unique element $z^{y}$ in K such that

$$
z y = (z \cdot y) z ^ {y}.
$$

(1.2)

Let $y,y^{\prime}$ be elements of H and $z,z^{\prime}$ be elements of K. Expanding the associativity relations

$$
(z z ^ {\prime}) y = z \left(z ^ {\prime} y\right) \quad \text {a n d} \quad z \left(y y ^ {\prime}\right) = (z y) y ^ {\prime}
$$

gives us the relations

$$
\left(z z ^ {\prime}\right) \cdot y = z \cdot \left(z ^ {\prime} \cdot y\right),
$$

(1.3)

$$
\left(z z ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {y} = z ^ {z ^ {\prime}, y} z ^ {\prime \prime}, y
$$

(1.4)

$$
z \cdot \left(y y ^ {\prime}\right) = (z \cdot y) \left(z ^ {y} \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right),
$$

(1.5)

(1.6)

$$
z ^ {y y ^ {\prime}} = \left(z ^ {y}\right) ^ {y ^ {\prime}}.
$$

Similarly, we expand $z=z1$ and $y=1y$ , which implies

$$
z \cdot 1 = 1,
$$

(1.7)

$$
z ^ {1} = z,
$$

(1.8)

$$
1 \cdot y = y,
$$

(1.9)

$$
1 ^ {y} = 1.
$$

(1.10)

Relations (1.3) and (1.9) mean precisely that the map $\alpha : K\times H\to H$ defined by

$$
\alpha (z, y) = z \cdot y
$$

is a left action of the group K on the set H. Similarly (1.6) and (1.8) mean that the map $\beta: K\times H\to K$ defined by

$$
\beta (z, y) = z ^ {y}
$$

is a left action of the group K on the set H. Similarly (1.6) and (1.8) mean that the map $\beta: K\times H\to K$ defined by

$$
\beta (z, y) = z ^ {y}
$$

is a right action of the group H on the set K. We make the following definition.

Definition IX.1.1. A pair (H, K) of groups is said to be matched if there exist a left action $\alpha$ of the group K on the set H and a right action $\beta$ of the group H on the set K, such that for all y,y' $\in$ H and z,z' $\in$ K we have

$$
\left(z z ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {y} = z ^ {z ^ {\prime} \cdot y} z ^ {\prime y},
$$

(1.4)

$$
z \cdot \left(y y ^ {\prime}\right) = (z \cdot y) \left(z ^ {y} \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right),
$$

(1.5)

$$
z \cdot 1 = 1,
$$

(1.7)

$$
1 ^ {y} = 1,
$$

(1.10)

$\alpha(z, y) = z \cdot y$ and $\beta(z, y) = z^y$.

Proposition IX.1.2. (a) Let $(H, K )$ be a matched pair of groups. There exists a unique group structure, denoted $H \bowtie K$ , on the set-theoretic product $H \times K$ with unit (1,1) such that

$$
(y, z) \left(y ^ {\prime}, z ^ {\prime}\right) = \left(y \left(z \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right), z ^ {y ^ {\prime}} z ^ {\prime}\right)
$$

for all y, $y^{\prime}\in H$ and z, $z^{\prime}\in K.$ This group structure is called the bicrossed product of H and K . Furthermore, the groups H and K can be identified respectively with the subgroups $H\times\{1\}$ and $\{1\}\times K$ of $H\bowtie K,$ and every element (y,z) in $H\bowtie K$ can be written uniquely as the product of an element of $H\times\{1\}$ and an element of $\{1\}\times K:$

$$
(y, z) = (y, 1) (1, z)
$$

y ∈ H and z ∈ K.

(b) Conversely, let $G$ be a group and $H, K$ be subgroups of $G$ such that the multiplication on $G$ induces a set-theoretic bijection from $H \times K$ onto $G.$ Then the pair $(H, K)$ is necessarily matched and the previous bijection induces a group isomorphism from the bicrossed product $H \bowtie K$ onto $G.$

PROOF. (a) It is easy to check that the above-defined product on $H \bowtie K$ is associative with (1,1) as unit. Details are left to the reader.

To prove that $( y,z)$ is invertible in the bicrossed product, let us first look for elements $y^{\prime}\in H$ and $z^{\prime}\in K$ such that

$$
(y, z) \left(y ^ {\prime}, z ^ {\prime}\right) = (1, 1).
$$

By definition of the product, this is equivalent to the following two relations:

$$
(y, z) \left(y ^ {\prime}, z ^ {\prime}\right) = (1, 1).
$$

By definition of the product, this is equivalent to the following two relations:

$$
y \left(z \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) = 1 \quad \text {a n d} \quad z ^ {y ^ {\prime}} z ^ {\prime} = 1.
$$

From the first one we derive

$$
y ^ {\prime} = z ^ {- 1} \cdot \left(z \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) = z ^ {- 1} \cdot y ^ {- 1},
$$

and then from the second one we get

$$
z ^ {\prime} = \left(z ^ {z ^ {- 1} \cdot y ^ {- 1}}\right) ^ {- 1}.
$$

Set $( y^{\prime}, z^{\prime} ) ( y,z)=(Y,Z)$ where $y^{\prime}$ and $z^{\prime}$ are given the above values. We have to show that $( Y,Z)=(1,1)$ . Multiplying the last identity by $( y,z)$ on the left, we get

$$
(y, z) = (y, z) (Y, Z) = \left(y \left(z \cdot Y\right), z ^ {Y} Z\right).
$$

This implies that

$$
Y = z ^ {- 1} \cdot (z \cdot Y) = z ^ {- 1} \cdot 1 = 1 \quad \mathrm {a n d} \quad Z = z ^ {Y} z ^ {- 1} = z ^ {1} z ^ {- 1} = 1.
$$

Thus, the element $(y,z)$ is invertible with inverse equal to

$$
(y, z) ^ {- 1} = \left(z ^ {- 1} \cdot y ^ {- 1}, \left(z ^ {z ^ {- 1} \cdot y ^ {- 1}}\right) ^ {- 1}\right).
$$

It is easy to check that

$$
(y, 1) \left(y ^ {\prime}, 1\right) = \left(y y ^ {\prime}, 1\right), \quad (1, z) \left(1, z ^ {\prime}\right) = \left(1, z z ^ {\prime}\right) \quad \text {a n d} \quad (y, 1) (1, z) = (y, z),
$$

which proves the remaining assertions of Part (a).

For the proof of Part (b), it suffices to review the arguments that led us to Definition 1.1.

Example 1. (Product of groups) Let H and K be groups. We let each one act trivially on the other, which means, using the above notation, that

$$
z \cdot y = y \quad \text {a n d} \quad z ^ {y} = z.
$$

Then $(H, K)$ is a matched pair, and the bicrossed product $H \bowtie K$ is isomorphic to the usual product of groups $H \times K$.

Example 2. (Semidirect product of groups) Let H and K be groups. We suppose that H acts trivially on K, which means that $z^{y}=z$ , and that K acts on H by group automorphisms, which means that

$$
z \cdot \left(y y ^ {\prime}\right) = \left(z \cdot y\right) \left(z \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) \quad \text {a n d} \quad z \cdot 1 = 1
$$

$$
z \cdot \left(y y ^ {\prime}\right) = \left(z \cdot y\right) \left(z \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) \quad \text {a n d} \quad z \cdot 1 = 1
$$

for all $y, y^{\prime} \in H$ and $z \in K.$ Then $(H,K)$ is a matched pair and the bicrossed product $H \bowtie K$ is isomorphic to the semidirect product of $K$ by $H.$ In this case, the identity $(1,z)(y,1)(1,z)^{-1} = ((z \cdot y),1)$ proves that $H \times \{1\}$ is a normal subgroup of $H \bowtie K$ and that the action of $K$ on $H$ corresponds to the conjugation in the bicrossed product.

## IX.2 Bicrossed Products of Bialgebras

We observed in Chapter III that the algebra of a group has a natural Hopf algebra structure. The question we raise now is this: Given a matched pair $(H, K)$ of groups, can we build the algebra of the bicrossed product $H \bowtie K$ out of the group algebras $k[H]$ and $k[K]?$ In order to answer this question, we first give a group algebra version of the action of a group on a set. Let us consider the case of a group G acting on a set X via a map

$$
\alpha : G \times X \rightarrow X.
$$

Linearizing, we get a morphism of coalgebras

$$
\alpha : k [ G \times X ] \rightarrow k [ X ]
$$

for the coalgebra structures introduced in III.1, Example 3. Composing with the natural isomorphism

$$
k [ G ] \otimes k [ X ] \cong k [ G \times X ],
$$

which is a coalgebra isomorphism by Proposition III.1.4, we see that the group action of G on the set X gives rise to an action of the Hopf algebra $k[G]$ on the coalgebra $k[X]$ such that the structural map

$$
k [ G ] \otimes k [ X ] \rightarrow k [ X ]
$$

is a morphism of coalgebras. The coalgebra $k[X]$ is thus a module-coalgebra on the Hopf algebra $k[G]$ in the sense of the following definition.

Definition IX.2.1. Let H be a bialgebra and C be a coalgebra. We say that C is a module-coalgebra over H if there exists a morphism of coalgebras $H \otimes C \to C$ inducing an H-module structure on C.

We are ready to give the definition of a matched pair of bialgebras.

Definition IX.2.2. A pair (X,A) of bialgebras is matched if there exist linear maps $\alpha: A\otimes X\to X$ and $\beta: A\otimes X\to A$ turning X into a module-coalgebra over A, and turning A into a right module-coalgebra over X, such that, if we set

$$
\alpha (a \otimes x) = a \cdot x \quad a n d \quad \beta (a \otimes x) = a ^ {x},
$$

the following conditions are satisfied:

$$
a \cdot (x y) = \sum_ {(a) (x)} \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot x ^ {\prime}\right) \left(a ^ {\prime \prime} x ^ {\prime \prime} \cdot y\right),
$$

(2.1)

$$
a \cdot 1 = \varepsilon (a) 1,
$$

(2.2)

(2.1)

$$
a \cdot 1 = \varepsilon (a) 1,
$$

(2.2)

$$
(a b) ^ {x} = \sum_ {(b) (x)} a ^ {b ^ {\prime} \cdot x ^ {\prime}} b ^ {\prime \prime x ^ {\prime \prime}},
$$

(2.3)

$$
1 ^ {x} = \varepsilon (x) 1,
$$

(2.4)

$$
\sum_ {(a) (x)} a ^ {\prime x ^ {\prime}} \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime} \cdot x ^ {\prime \prime} = \sum_ {(a) (x)} a ^ {\prime \prime x ^ {\prime \prime}} \otimes a ^ {\prime} \cdot x ^ {\prime}
$$

(2.5)

for all a,b ∈ A and x,y ∈ X.

Observe that Condition (2.5) is automatically satisfied when both bialgebras A and X are cocommutative. We also remark that Definition 2.2 is an immediate generalization of Definition 1.1. As a basic example of a matched pair of bialgebras, we may take the pair $( k[H],k[K] )$ of group bialgebras where $( H, K)$ is a matched pair of groups.

The maps $\alpha$ and $\beta$ being morphisms of coalgebras, we have

$$
\Delta (a \cdot x) = \sum_ {(a) (x)} a ^ {\prime} \cdot x ^ {\prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime} \cdot x ^ {\prime \prime} \quad \mathrm {a n d} \quad \varepsilon (a \cdot x) = \varepsilon (a) \varepsilon (x) 1
$$

(2.6)

in X, and

$$
\Delta \left(a ^ {x}\right) = \sum_ {(a) (x)} a ^ {\prime x ^ {\prime}} \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime x ^ {\prime \prime}} \quad \text {a n d} \quad \varepsilon \left(a ^ {x}\right) = \varepsilon (a) \varepsilon (x) 1
$$

(2.7)

in A. We state the main result of this section; it is a natural extension of Proposition 1.2.

Theorem IX.2.3. Let $( X, A )$ be a matched pair of bialgebras. There exists a unique bialgebra structure on the vector space $X \otimes A$ , with unit equal to $1\otimes1$ , such that its product is given by

$$
(x \otimes a) (y \otimes b) = \sum_ {(a) (y)} x \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime} y ^ {\prime \prime} b,
$$

its coproduct by

$$
\Delta (x \otimes a) = \sum_ {(a) (x)} \left(x ^ {\prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime}\right) \otimes \left(x ^ {\prime \prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime}\right),
$$

and its counit by

$$
\varepsilon (x \otimes a) = \varepsilon (x) \varepsilon (a)
$$

and its counit by

$$
\varepsilon (x \otimes a) = \varepsilon (x) \varepsilon (a)
$$

for all x,y $\in X$ and a,b $\in A.$ Equipped with this bialgebra structure, $X\otimes A$ is called the bicrossed product of X and A and denoted $X\bowtie A.$ Furthermore, the injective maps $i_{X}(x)=x\otimes 1$ and $i_{A}(a)=1\otimes a$ from X and from A into $X\bowtie A$ are bialgebra morphisms. We also have

$$
x \otimes a = (x \otimes 1) (1 \otimes a)
$$

for a ∈ A and x ∈ X.

If the bialgebras X and A have antipodes, respectively denoted $S_{X}$ and $S_{A}$ , then the bicrossed product is a Hopf algebra with antipode S given by

$$
S (x \otimes a) = \sum_ {(x) (a)} S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \cdot S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime}\right)}.
$$

Proof. The above formulas show that we equipped the bicrossed product with the coalgebra structure of the tensor product of coalgebras $X$ and $A.$ It is then clear that $i_{X}$ and $i_{A}$ are coalgebra morphisms. It remains to be proved that $X \bowtie A$ has an algebra structure and that the coproduct and the counit, as well as the embeddings $i_{X}$ and $i_{A},$ are algebra morphisms.

Let us start with the associativity of the product. An easy but tedious computation using Relations (2.1) and (2.3) and the fact that both $\alpha$ and

$\beta$ are coalgebra morphisms, shows that if x,y,z $\in X$ and a,b,c $\in A$ , then both

$$
\left((x \otimes a) (y \otimes b)\right) (z \otimes c) \quad \text {a n d} \quad (x \otimes a) \left((y \otimes b) (z \otimes c)\right)
$$

are equal to

$$
\sum_ {(a) (b) (y) (z)} x \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) \left(\left(a ^ {\prime \prime y ^ {\prime \prime}} b ^ {\prime}\right) \cdot z ^ {\prime}\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime \prime y ^ {\prime \prime \prime} \left(b ^ {\prime \prime} \cdot z ^ {\prime \prime}\right)} b ^ {\prime \prime \prime z ^ {\prime \prime}} c.
$$

For the unit we get, using (2.2) and (2.4),

$$
(1 \otimes 1) (x \otimes a) = \sum_ {(x)} \left(1 \cdot x ^ {\prime}\right) \otimes 1 ^ {x ^ {\prime \prime}} a = \sum_ {(x)} x ^ {\prime} \otimes \varepsilon \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) a = \sum_ {(x)} x ^ {\prime} \varepsilon \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \otimes a = x \otimes a
$$

and

$$
(x \otimes a) (1 \otimes 1) = \sum_ {(a)} x \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot 1\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime 1} = \sum_ {(a)} x \varepsilon \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime} = \sum_ {(a)} x \otimes \varepsilon \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) a ^ {\prime \prime} = x \otimes a.
$$

Let us prove that the counit is a morphism of algebras. We have to check that

$$
\varepsilon \left(\left(x \otimes a\right) \left(y \otimes b\right)\right) = \varepsilon \left(x \otimes a\right) \varepsilon \left(y \otimes b\right) = \varepsilon (x) \varepsilon (a) \varepsilon (y) \varepsilon (b).
$$

Now the left-hand side is equal to

\begin{array}{l} \varepsilon \left(\sum_ {(a) (y)} x \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime y ^ {\prime \prime}} b\right) = \sum_ {(a) (y)} \varepsilon (x) \varepsilon \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) \varepsilon \left(a ^ {\prime \prime y ^ {\prime \prime}}\right) \varepsilon (b) \\ = \varepsilon (x) \varepsilon (b) \left(\sum_ {(a) (y)} \varepsilon \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) \varepsilon \left(y ^ {\prime}\right) \varepsilon \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \varepsilon \left(y ^ {\prime \prime}\right)\right) \\ = \varepsilon (x) \varepsilon (b) \varepsilon (a) \varepsilon (y) \\ \end{array}
$$

in view of (2.6) and (2.7). To conclude, we show that Relation (2.5) implies that the coproduct is a morphism of algebras. We have

$$
\Delta (x \otimes a) \Delta (y \otimes b) = \sum_ {(x) (a) (y) (b)} x ^ {\prime} \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime y ^ {\prime \prime}} b ^ {\prime} \otimes x ^ {\prime \prime} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime \prime} \cdot y ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime y ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime}} b ^ {\prime \prime},
$$

$$
\Delta \left((x \otimes a) (y \otimes b)\right) = \sum_ {(x) (a) (y) (b)} x ^ {\prime} \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot y ^ {\prime}\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime \prime y ^ {\prime \prime \prime}} b ^ {\prime} \otimes x ^ {\prime \prime} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime} \cdot y ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime y ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime}} b ^ {\prime \prime}.
$$

Both expressions are equal in view of Relation (2.5).

Now suppose that A and X have antipodes. We have to check that the formula

$$
S (x \otimes a) = \sum_ {(x) (a)} S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \cdot S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime}\right)}
$$
defines an antipode on the bialgebra $X \bowtie A$ . Using the fact that $S_{A}$ and $S_{X}$ are antipodes, we get

\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {(x) (a)} \left(x ^ {\prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime}\right) S \left(x ^ {\prime \prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} \left(x ^ {\prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime}\right) \left(S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right) \cdot S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right) \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right)}\right) \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} x ^ {\prime} \left(\left(a ^ {\prime} S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right)\right) \cdot S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right)\right) \otimes \left(a ^ {\prime \prime} S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right)\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right)} \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} x ^ {\prime} \left(\left(a ^ {\prime} S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right)\right) \cdot S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right)\right) \otimes \varepsilon \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \varepsilon \left(S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right)\right) 1 \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} x ^ {\prime} \left(\left(a ^ {\prime} S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right)\right) \cdot S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right)\right) \otimes 1 \\ = \varepsilon (a) \left(\sum_ {(x)} x ^ {\prime} S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \otimes 1\right) \\ = \varepsilon

\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {(x) (a)} S \left(x ^ {\prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime}\right) \left(x ^ {\prime \prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} \left(S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \cdot S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime}\right)}\right) \left(x ^ {\prime \prime \prime} \otimes a ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right) \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} \left(S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right) \cdot S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right)\right) \left(S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right)} \cdot x ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime}\right) \\ \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime}\right) x ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime}} a ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime} \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \cdot \left(S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) x ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right) \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime}\right) x ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime}} a ^ {\prime \prime \prime} \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} \varepsilon \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \left(S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \cdot 1\right) \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {S _

(a)} \varepsilon \left(x ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \left(S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \cdot 1\right) \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime}\right) x ^ {\prime \prime \prime}} a ^ {\prime \prime \prime} \\ = \sum_ {(x) (a)} \varepsilon \left(S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right)\right) 1 \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {S _ {X} \left(x ^ {\prime}\right) x ^ {\prime \prime \prime}} a ^ {\prime \prime \prime} \\ = \varepsilon (x) \sum_ {(a)} 1 \otimes S _ {A} \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {1} a ^ {\prime \prime} \\ = \varepsilon (x) \varepsilon (a) 1 \otimes 1 \\ = \varepsilon (x \otimes a) 1 \otimes 1
. \\ \end{array}

We conclude this section with three examples.

Example 1. As already observed, if $( H, K )$ is a matched pair of groups, then the pair $( k[H],k[K] )$ is a matched pair of bialgebras. Furthermore, the group algebra of the bicrossed product is isomorphic to the bicrossed product of the group algebras

$$
k [ H \bowtie K ] \cong k [ H ] \bowtie k [ K ].
$$

Example 2. (Tensor product of bialgebras) Let X and A be bialgebras. We let each one act trivially on the other one by

$$

## IX.3 Variations on the Adjoint Representation

Let $( H, \mu, \eta, \Delta, \varepsilon, S)$ be a Hopf algebra. If a and x are elements of H, we set

$$
a \cdot x = \sum_ {(a)} a ^ {\prime} x S \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \quad \text {a n d} \quad x ^ {a} = \sum_ {(a)} S \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) x a ^ {\prime \prime}.

Proposition IX.3.1. The map $(a,x) \mapsto a \cdot x$ endows $H$ with the structure of a left module-algebra on the bialgebra $H$. We denote by $_{ad}H$ the thus

defined H-module, and we call this action the left adjoint representation of H. Similarly, the map $(x,a)\mapsto x^{a}$ endows H with the structure of a right module-algebra on the bialgebra H. We denote by $H_{ad}$ the H-module defined this way, and we call this action the right adjoint representation of H.

Proof. We give the proof for the left adjoint representation. We first check that $( a,x)\mapsto a\cdot x$ puts an H-module structure on H. Indeed, we have $1\cdot x=x$ and

$$
b \cdot (a \cdot x) = \sum_ {(a) (b)} b ^ {\prime} a ^ {\prime} x S \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) S \left(b ^ {\prime \prime}\right) = \sum_ {(b a)} \left(b a\right) ^ {\prime} x S \left(\left(b a\right) ^ {\prime \prime}\right) = (b a) \cdot x
$$

for all a,b,x $\in$ H. Let us show it is a module-algebra over H. We have

$$
a \cdot 1 = \sum_ {(a)} a ^ {\prime} S \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) = \varepsilon (a) 1
$$

and

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {(a)} \left(a ^ {\prime} \cdot x\right) \left(a ^ {\prime \prime} \cdot y\right) = \sum_ {(a)} a ^ {\prime} x S \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) a ^ {\prime \prime \prime} y S \left(a ^ {\prime \prime \prime \prime}\right) \\ = \sum_ {(a)} a ^ {\prime} x \varepsilon \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) y S \left(a ^ {\prime \prime \prime}\right) \\ = \sum_ {(a)} a ^ {\prime} x y S \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \\ = a \cdot (x y). \\ \end{array}
$$

Example 1. (Conjugacy in a group) Let G be a group and $k[G]$ be the corresponding Hopf algebra. The left adjoint representation of $k[G]$ is given by the formula

$$
a \cdot x = a x a ^ {- 1}
$$

for a, x $\in G.$

Example 2. (Adjoint representation of a Lie algebra) Let L be a Lie algebra and U(L) be its enveloping algebra equipped with its canonical Hopf algebra structure (see V.2). The left adjoint representation of U(L) is given by the formula

$$
a \cdot x = a x - x a
$$

for a, x $\in$ L. The corresponding representation of L is called the adjoint representation of the Lie algebra L.
